## The Keras Decompression Bomb Vulnerability

A proof-of-concept for this vulnerability was published on Hugging Face. The core issue is in Keras's model-loading code:

keras/src/saving/saving_lib.py's _load_model_from_fileobj reads the attacker-supplied model.weights.h5 ZIP member into memory with no preflight check on its declared uncompressed size, using io_file = io.BytesIO(zf.open(_VARS_FNAME_H5, "r").read()). The only preceding gate, is_memory_sufficient(model), inspects the attacker-controlled config.json only.

### How the Attack Works

The gate that's supposed to protect against oversized loads is trivially bypassed. An attacker who declares a 1-parameter model passes the gate trivially, then attaches a ZIP_DEFLATED-bombed model.weights.h5 member that decompresses at the zlib theoretical max of ~1,032:1. A 1.0 MB upload produces ~1.04 GB of RSS growth in keras.saving.load_model() — a 1,043× amplification, verified empirically.

The attack scales linearly: scaling to ~4 MB on disk yields ~4.3 GB of RSS.

### Affected Versions & Classification

This affects keras 3.14.1 (PyPI) and keras-team/keras master 6d4b584. It is classified as CWE-409 (Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data — Data Amplification) with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H).

### Context on the File Format

For background, the `.keras` file that's being exploited is a zip archive. It consists of a JSON-based configuration file (config.json) recording model, layer, and other trackables' configuration; a H5-based state file such as model.weights.h5 (for the whole model), with directory keys for layers and their weights; and a metadata file in JSON, storing things such as the current Keras version. The vulnerability exploits the fact that the config.json is checked but the H5 weights member (which the bomb targets) is not size-validated before decompression.

### General Note on Decompression Bombs

This fits the classic pattern of decompression bombs. The ZIP format's design allows references to large content that is only materialized during unpacking. The decompression process allocates memory and disk for all data before passing control back to the calling application, so systems that don't enforce limits quickly run out of resources.
